title: Purim: hearing Esther
hookLine: the whole scroll read, with noise at Haman's name
tomorrow: why does Purim send you to two poor people?

cards: Skipping an episode can wreck a whole series. On Purim, the Book of Esther is read from a scroll, the Megillah, and the rule is to hear every word.

When the villain Haman's name comes up, the room erupts, rattles, stamping, booing, to blot it out. Then silence, so the next words can be heard. And the scroll has a strange feature for a book of the Bible.
In the Hebrew, God is never named.

teach.b: So today's question: can God be in a story that never says God's name? The rabbis answer with a play on Esther's name. They hear in it the Hebrew of a line from Deuteronomy: "I will surely hide My face."
A hidden God, working through palace gossip, a sleepless king, a dinner at the right moment. That's why the reading has a rule.
The Mishnah says that if you read the scroll out of order, you haven't done it. Every word, in sequence, because the hand only shows in the whole chain. That's why the noise stops.
In the King James Bible, Mordecai's question to Esther runs: "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
The shared ground is real: a young woman who risks the palace to save her people, and a question about why you're standing where you are. And an honest difference.
Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra chapters from the Greek, in which Mordecai and Esther pray aloud and God is named.
Protestant Bibles set those chapters apart, among the Apocrypha. The Hebrew scroll keeps its silence. The same story, heard two ways, and each tradition keeps its own.

how: On Purim, Jews hear the Megillah, the scroll of Esther, read aloud in the evening and again in the morning, following along word by word and making noise with groggers or stamping at Haman's name.

games.q: at the Purim reading, the kids are so loud after Haman's name that you miss the next sentence. what's the rule?
o: it's fine; the noise is the commandment.
you need every word, so you catch up on what you missed.
you only need the main story, not every line.
games.why: the noise blots out Haman, then stops so every word can be heard. the commandment is the whole scroll, in order.

practice: For the sit, listen to your breath as a story told in order: the start of the inhale, its middle, the turn, the long way out. Don't skip ahead to the end of any breath.
If a noise interrupts, let it, then come back for the next word, the way the room goes quiet after Haman.

wordCard.voice: Purim: lots. Haman "cast pur, that is, the lot," to pick a day; the festival is named for it, and the whole scroll is heard.

orig.note: Hebrew: scroll; on Purim, the scroll of Esther.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: hear it all. Every word, in order, even the quiet ones where God is hiding.
